lesson.title: The Resolver That Does the Legwork for You
lesson.summary: A recursive resolver is the server that walks the DNS hierarchy on a client's behalf, turning one simple question from a device into a chain of lookups against the root, a TLD, and an authoritative server.
lesson.body:
Your laptop or phone does not walk the DNS tree itself. When an application asks for www.example.com, the operating system's stub resolver sends one question to a recursive resolver, usually run by an ISP or a public service, and then just waits for a single, final answer. All of the work described in the hierarchy chapter, tracing from the root down through a TLD to the domain that actually holds the record, happens on the recursive resolver's side, not the client's.

It helps to separate two kinds of DNS questions. The client's question to the recursive resolver is recursive: give me the final answer, or tell me it does not exist, and do whatever work is required to get there. The recursive resolver's questions to everyone else in the chain are iterative: give me your best answer right now, even if that answer is just a pointer to somewhere else to ask. Root and TLD servers only ever answer iteratively. Only the recursive resolver commits to doing the full recursive walk.

Trace an actual lookup for www.example.com assuming nothing is cached yet. The resolver first asks a root name server for www.example.com. The root server does not know the answer, but it knows who runs the com TLD, so it replies with a referral: the names and addresses of the com TLD servers. The resolver then asks a com TLD server the same question. The TLD server does not know the final answer either, but it does know, from the NS records in the previous chapter, which name servers are authoritative for example.com, so it replies with a referral to ns1.example.com and ns2.example.com. The resolver then asks ns1.example.com directly, and this time it gets a real, authoritative answer: an A record showing www.example.com at 192.0.2.10. The resolver hands that address back to the client, and the client finally has what it needed to open a connection.

A production recursive resolver is doing this for a huge number of clients at once, so it caches every answer it learns along the way, root referrals, TLD referrals, and final answers alike, according to each record's time to live. That caching is what keeps the full three hop walk from happening on every single lookup, and it is the subject of its own chapter shortly. For now, the key idea is the division of labor: the client asks once, the recursive resolver walks the tree, and the authoritative server at the bottom of that walk supplies the real answer.
